A global winner would itself count against the thesis that mobility is not one thing; the absence of one is what motivates the sub-regime partition. The selection of @sec-rp bears on this result in a specific direction: because it enriches the local sample with the short proximity-obeying moves that the graded metrics fit and binary cannot, it pushes the pooled race toward a spurious graded winner, against the no-dominance prior rather than with it. A pooled result of no dominance is therefore conservative, having survived a selection that works to manufacture the global winner it denies. We correspondingly do not assert pooled graded dominance as a finding: were a graded metric to clear the threshold pooled, the selection is a sufficient account of it, and we would report it as classification- and selection-dependent rather than as evidence that one geometry governs local mobility globally.

Fourth, the lift adjustment improves the fit of both skill and hierarchy on the local data and does not improve it on the non-local data. On the local side the adjustment removes leaked non-local transitions, the long credential-driven moves that the cost metrics assign low probability and whose presence degrades their fit, so their peak rises. On the non-local side the adjustment adds rescued wormholes and removes non-activating moves, if anything making the sample more movement-heavy, so skill and hierarchy fit it no better and may fit it worse. The prediction is therefore that the local-versus-non-local gap for these metrics widens under adjustment, strengthening the dissociation.

Fifth, the lift adjustment does not help the binary metric on either sample. The transitions the adjustment moves between samples are off-diagonal moves, and binary does not model where movers go, so shuffling them changes neither its local nor its non-local fit. This is the control that makes the fourth prediction interpretable: the adjustment moves the structured metrics and leaves binary fixed, the same dissociation the first two predictions establish, seen a second time through the reclassification.

### Predictions for the sub-regime grids {#sec-subregime-predictions}

Within the local sample we score all three metrics on each of the three OES sub-regime subsets, the full three-by-three grid, and we do this under both the proxy and the lift-adjusted classifications, yielding two grids. We commit to the following.

First, on the diagonal each metric wins its own subset: skill in the Skill subset, hierarchy in the Hierarchy subset, binary in the Binary subset. Binary winning its own subset is a substantive result, the claim that where human capital is occupation-specific no distance geometry orders destinations, not a null.

Second, off the diagonal each metric fails away from its own subset. The winner tracking the diagonal as the subset changes is the within-local dissociation; a metric that led across the whole grid would show no regime dependence and would count against the thesis.

Third, the two grids exist to guard against a specific bias, not as a generic robustness check. Undetected leakage of non-local transitions into the local sample favours the binary metric, since a leaked wormhole is a long move that degrades skill and hierarchy while binary, making no off-diagonal bet, is unchanged (@sec-rp). Running both classifications is what makes this bias visible and correctable: the proxy grid carries the leakage, the lift-adjusted grid removes the part of it that leaves a lift signature, and the difference between the grids is the signature of the bias. That signature is committed in advance, skill and hierarchy rise and binary stays flat under adjustment, never the reverse; its location is not. A subset stable across the two grids is uncontaminated; a subset where the structured metrics rise is where leakage sorted. We do not presume leakage concentrates in any particular subset, since no origin-OES mechanism predicts that it should; we measure where it sorts.

Fourth, the adjustment corrects only the detectable leakage. The reclassification fires on a lift signature, so leaks that leave none, a credential that activated but carried the worker into an occupation it does not distinctively feed, remain in both grids. The proxy-versus-adjusted difference is therefore a lower bound on the total leakage, and the adjusted grid is de-contaminated but not clean. The residual signature-less leakage is handled not by the reclassification but by the residual-bias argument of @sec-rp, which shows it biases conservatively.

Fifth, we pre-commit to the reading of the Binary subset, where the favouring-binary bias would most damage a result we care about. If binary's win there narrows under adjustment but still clears the ten percent threshold, the win is robust against detectable leakage and against sparse-cell noise per @sec-AE, with the residual signature-less leakage arguing conservatively per @sec-rp rather than removed. If binary's win does not survive adjustment, the detectable leakage alone was enough to manufacture it, and we report the Binary subset's result as classification-dependent rather than claiming binary governs there. The don't-survive reading is decisive; the survive reading carries the residual caveat.

As a worker-level extension of the same logic, we pre-register a partition on age in place of OES, reported at access. The specificity OES reads at the level of the occupation has a counterpart in the individual career. Early on, when little occupation-specific capital has accumulated, the binding constraint on mobility is capability, and moves run along skill adjacency, near in skill space while dispersed across silos. By mid-career the worker has settled into a silo and moves within it, so the binding constraint is the silo boundary that hierarchical distance prices. Late in the career the reservation wage has risen far enough that few moves clear it and the survivors carry no systematic geometry, the condition the binary model describes. We cut the worker age distribution at 15 to 25, 25 to 40, and 40 and over, fixed in advance, and predict the winning metric shifts across these bands in the order skill, hierarchy, binary. The prediction is the order of the shift, not its sharpness. Age reaches the governing constraint only as a proxy for a proxy, the worker's clock for tenure and tenure for accumulated specific capital, and each band is internally heterogeneous in career stage, so we expect the partition to resolve mobility far less decisively than OES and margins within any band may be thin. A confirmation of the ordering through so degraded an instrument is independent corroboration of the specificity mechanism rather than a second decisive result; the disconfirming outcomes are a different order, no ordering, or a winner that does not move across the bands. The oldest band is populous in workers but sparse in moves, since the move rate falls with age, so we read its binary result only against the sparse-cell power check of @sec-AE, which establishes whether a graded signal of the size seen in the younger bands would have been detectable there had it been present.

### Out-of-Regime Falsification {#sec-local-falsification}

The falsification scores $\Delta CWTVD$ under a single neutral cost matrix
rather than under the two informative judges used to adjudicate the race.
That matrix is $C$, the arithmetic mean of the three normalized cost
matrices $C_{\text{skill}}$, $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$, and
$C_{\text{binary}}$, in which no candidate geometry is privileged. The race
needs two judges because it resolves a close comparative contest between
correlated geometries, and bracketing the blend family is what certifies a
winner across it. The falsification needs the opposite: not a comparison
but a single fixed line that a predicted metric either crosses or does not.
A neutral blend supplies exactly one such line, and scoring the crossing
under two judges instead would reintroduce the grey zone the fixed line is
meant to remove. This is the one role for which the blend, retired from
adjudication, remains the right instrument.

The out-of-regime criterion is stated against independence, on this
neutral geometry-aware measure. In regime, the predicted winning metric,
$C_{\mathrm{skill}}$ in the Skill sub-regime and $C_{\mathrm{hierarchy}}$
in the Hierarchy sub-regime, peaks above independence on $\Delta KL$
and on $\Delta CWTVD$ under the neutral blend, since its geometry
rationalizes the transitions and improvement over independence is what the
horse race measures. Out of regime, where a new highest attainment resets
the worker's position and renders the 2016 occupation uninformative, that
metric is predicted to fall below independence on $\Delta CWTVD$.
 
The out-of-regime criterion rests on $\Delta CWTVD$ alone, and the reason
is that $\Delta KL$ cannot register the failure being tested. The
falsification asks whether the predicted metric has made the wrong
geometric bet, placing mass at the wrong distances. $\Delta CWTVD$ weights
each misallocation by distance and so penalises exactly this, falling below
independence when a short-move metric meets a movement-heavy matrix.
$\Delta KL$ is blind to geometry and scores any plan that captures the
diagonal stay/move structure, which every metric shares. A wrong-geometry
metric therefore collects partial KL credit for the diagonal even while its
off-diagonal bet is wrong, and its peak $\Delta KL$ can sit slightly above
independence rather than below it. This is visible in the simulations: in
the [online companion](https://rpmartin.github.io/not-one-thing-companion), under a binary data-generating process the skill and
hierarchy metrics peak below independence on $\Delta CWTVD$ but rise to a
small positive peak on $\Delta KL$ at moderate $\varepsilon$. Requiring the
geometry-blind measure to confirm a geometric failure would ask the wrong
instrument to register it. We therefore state the out-of-regime criterion
on $\Delta CWTVD$, the measure built to see what the falsification is about.
 
Setting the line at independence rather than at binary discharges the
conditionality that a binary benchmark would leave open. A wrongly
predicting metric always sits below binary out of regime, but whether its
$\Delta CWTVD$ also falls below independence depends on the non-local
transition matrix being movement-heavy: only when most credential-changers
move, and move far, does a short-move metric place enough mass on vacated
near pairs to fit worse than independence. We predict the non-local matrix
is movement-heavy, because the wormhole mechanism is precisely the claim
that a new credential drives long discontinuous jumps. The
below-independence criterion therefore tests two things at once. Its
crossing requires both that the predicted metric makes the wrong geometric
bet out of regime and that the non-local matrix is movement-heavy as the
mechanism predicts, so a metric whose $\Delta CWTVD$ falls below zero
jointly falsifies the local model out of regime and confirms the long-jump
prediction. A metric that stayed above independence out of regime would
either be governing where it should not or would reveal a non-local matrix
lighter than the mechanism requires, and either reading counts against the
design.
 
Independence is a fixed point, so the criterion is unambiguous. The
predicted metric's $\Delta CWTVD$ peak is either below zero or it is not,
with no margin to calibrate and no grey zone to adjudicate, where the race
resolves a close contest between two correlated geometries by asking
whether one peak exceeds the other by 10\%. The two sides of the
falsification are also weaker bars than winning the race. A metric clears
the in-regime side by improving on independence at all, and fails the
out-of-regime side by crossing below it; the race is won only by leading
every rival by 10\% on both measures. Both skill and hierarchy peak well
above independence in either of their sub-regimes, since they are
correlated and each partially rationalizes the other's transitions, yet
only one wins. Improving on independence is necessary for a geometry to be
governing at all; leading by 10\% on both measures is what crowns it.
 
The mechanism that drives the predicted metric's $\Delta CWTVD$ below
independence is the same one that makes binary a useful point of
comparison. All three cost matrices assign zero self-distance,
$C_{ii} = 0$, so all three concentrate mass on the diagonal and capture the
dominant stay/move feature of the transition matrix. That diagonal
contribution is common to every plan, and what distinguishes the metrics is
the off-diagonal allocation. Binary makes no off-diagonal bet, since every
switch is equidistant under it, so it cannot be wrong about where movers
go. Skill and hierarchy do make that bet, and out of regime it is the wrong
one, because they place mass on geometrically proximate pairs that wormhole
movers avoid while the data concentrates on far pairs. A metric predicting
short moves into a movement-heavy matrix withholds mass from exactly where
the data sits, and $\Delta CWTVD$ penalises that misallocation by distance,
driving it below independence. The signature of this failure on
$\Delta CWTVD$ is a curve that rises monotonically toward the independence
baseline from below without crossing it, improving as $\varepsilon$ grows
only because diffusion toward independence is the one thing that helps a
metric whose geometry points the wrong way.
 
The sub-regime models are falsified the same way, with one exception. In
regime each sub-regime is expected to produce a metric that peaks above
independence on both measures, and out of regime that metric's $\Delta
CWTVD$ peak is predicted to fall below independence. We apply this to the
Skill and Hierarchy sub-regimes only. The Binary sub-regime is exempt from
the distance-based out-of-regime test for a reason internal to its own
hypothesis, and the exemption does not depend on what its out-of-regime
cell turns out to contain. Its in-regime claim is that no distance geometry
governs, so it never generates a prediction that distance ceases to govern
out of regime; there is no distance bet to be caught making wrongly, with
or without movers in the cell. Separately, the lock-in mechanism that
defines the sub-regime predicts that cell is near-empty, because workers
already in a high-OES occupation rarely acquire a new highest attainment,
since occupation-specific human capital is reached through a single
credentialing pipeline and confers no incentive to re-credential. A
non-empty cell therefore falsifies the lock-in premise without thereby
reinstating a distance test the hypothesis never licensed: the
distance-based leg stays inapplicable, and the non-emptiness is read as
evidence against lock-in in its own right. The out-of-regime content of the Binary hypothesis otherwise lies on the
entry side and is carried by the destination-OES coefficient in the
non-local specificity regression rather than by a horse race.

## Non-Local Model {#sec-non_local}

The non-local model estimates the conditional-on-positive relationship between how far a worker travels through occupation space and the pipeline strength of their transition, measured by lift. We measure that distance two ways, with different estimators and complementary roles. The primary outcome is $\log(d_{ij})$, the log skill distance between 2016 and 2021 occupations, estimated by OLS. The second is a binary indicator for whether the move crosses an occupation broad group, a silo, estimated by a linear probability model (LPM). The hierarchical metric is ordinal, not cardinal: its values, one through the cross-category sentinel of nine, are ranks with an assigned spacing rather than real distances, so they cannot enter an OLS outcome as a graded distance. Its distribution is also dominated by the cross-category sentinel, with within-silo values a thin minority, so the one contrast with mass on both sides is whether a move crosses a silo at all. The binary cross-silo indicator is therefore the operational form the metric supports for non-local jumps.

<!-- The cross-silo margin is the right hierarchical form because of where high-lift destinations sit. A high-lift move is by construction a move into a credential-fed occupation, and credential-fed occupations are concentrated in the skilled silos rather than in the generic entry silos such as sales and service, which contain few. The high-lift destinations within sales and service are a small and specific set of licensed or skilled-service occupations, funeral directors, chefs, insurance and real-estate agents, each fed by a dedicated credential, while the generic occupations that make up most of the silo are reached at close to baseline prevalence from every education. A high-lift credential earned by a worker in the generic part of such a silo therefore has almost no within-silo destination to channel into, so the move it opens is cross-silo by the structure of where credentials lead rather than by the length of the jump. -->

The mechanism is directional: a wormhole is a path a credential opens through occupation space. A specific education channels workers toward a narrow set of occupations that would otherwise be unreachable, and the long jump occurs when a worker travels along that channel into the occupation the credential distinctively feeds. This is a property of the education--destination pair, not of either alone, and one quantity measures it: the lift $m(e,n) = P(n\mid e)/P(n)$ of the destination occupation $n$ for the worker's education $e$, defined in @sec-AB as the cell-level term of the education-side specificity divergence. Read directly rather than aggregated, it makes the conjunction requirement automatic: a generic education offers no high-lift path to take, and a specific credential whose holder lands off its distinctive path realizes low lift wherever else they go, so only travel along a genuine pipeline registers as high. 

Let $y_{ij}$ denote the outcome ($\log(d_{ij})$ in skill space, estimated by OLS, or the cross-silo indicator, estimated by LPM), and let $r_j$ be the destination's remoteness. The remoteness control is defined on the same scale as the outcome it accompanies, so it swaps with the outcome. For the OLS specification $r_j = \overline{\log d_j}$, the mean of $\log d_{ij}$ over origins $i \neq j$ with $d_{ij} > 0$: the destination's average log inbound distance, taken over the same positive-distance support the outcome is restricted to. For the LPM the control is the share of occupations lying outside $j$'s broad group, which is already on the outcome's scale and needs no transformation.

$$
y_{ij} = \alpha + \beta\, \log(m(e_i, j)) + \gamma r_j + \delta_i + \varepsilon_{ij}
$$ {#eq-lift}

The specification includes origin occupation fixed effects $\delta_i$ and a destination remoteness control $r_j$, but not destination fixed effects. The reason is structural, not one of feasibility. Lift is a property of the education--destination pair, so all workers who reach a given destination through the same education carry the identical lift; within a strong pipeline, where a destination is reached predominantly through one education, lift is very nearly constant, and the variation in distance among those workers comes from their differing origins, not from lift. Destination fixed effects would therefore identify the lift coefficient only from within-destination variation in lift, which is precisely what a pipeline lacks: the more exclusive the pipeline, the less within-destination lift variation it has, so destination fixed effects are blindest exactly where the mechanism is strongest. The identifying variation is between destinations, high-lift pipelines against low-lift ones, which is also what the wormhole claim is about. The remoteness control preserves that variation while netting out a confound of concern, a destination lying far from all others in skill space, or in a small broad group most origins fall outside, which registers long jumps mechanically with no credential mechanism involved. Conditioning on $r_j$ ensures the lift coefficient reflects credential-gated channeling rather than baseline remoteness. Origin remoteness needs no separate term; $\delta_i$ absorbs it with every other origin-level determinant of distance.

Whether $r_j$ is a control or part of the mechanism depends on what lift is taken to measure, and the two readings imply different estimands. Under the realized-path reading adopted here, lift scores the education--destination pair actually traversed, so a destination may be remote for reasons unconnected to credentials, an idiosyncratic skill profile or a small broad group most origins fall outside, and such a destination registers long jumps from any origin with no pipeline involved. That is a confound and $r_j$ removes it. Under an increment-specificity reading, in which lift stands in for how occupation-specific the acquired human capital is, remoteness would instead be a signature of the mechanism: an occupation reachable only through dedicated training might for that reason sit far from the origins workers arrive from, in which case $r_j$ would partial out the mechanism's own footprint. The readings are not distinguishable by inspection of $r_j$, which is a destination-level average and would absorb credential-driven and structural remoteness alike.

They are answerable from the public data, and we settle the question before VDL access rather than leaving it to a robustness pair. Lift decomposes exactly as $\log m(e,n) = \log P(n \mid e) - \log P(n)$, a concentration term and a rarity term, and the increment-specificity reading predicts that remoteness tracks one or both. We bring both to destination level from the unsmoothed education$\times$NOC table --- rarity as $\log P(n)$, concentration as the unresidualized KL divergence of $P(\text{education} \mid \text{NOC})$ from the education margin, deliberately not the size-residualized OES of @sec-cf, whose residualization on $\log(T)$ would render the two regressors near-orthogonal by construction --- and regress $r_j$ on the pair across the 498 destinations. Both enter positively and are individually distinguishable from zero, but jointly they account for about five percent of the variation in $r_j$, and rarity enters with the sign opposite to the one the increment-specificity reading predicts: more common occupations are marginally the more remote. The destinations with the largest positive residuals are occupations whose skill profiles are idiosyncratic in ways neither component of lift captures: air pilots, dancers and other performers, none of them narrowly fed in the census education margins. The occupations with the highest leverage on the two regressors, senior managers and general practitioners, sit near zero residual, so the fitted relationship is not driven by the extremes.

We read this as licensing $r_j$ in every specification rather than a with-and-without pair. What the control absorbs is overwhelmingly skill-space position unrelated to the education table, which is the confound the realized-path reading names; the components of lift explain almost none of it. The residual ambiguity is not eliminated --- five percent is not zero, and $\gamma$ retains whatever mechanism-through-remoteness it carries --- so we report $\gamma$ and read $\beta$ as the narrow channeling estimate rather than as the broader claim that credentials open paths to otherwise unreachable occupations. This diagnostic uses only public data and is reproducible from it; it is a specification choice made in the open before the firewall, not a result.

Both outcome specifications share the lift coefficient $\beta$, expected to be positive: travel along a stronger education--occupation pipeline is longer, and more likely to cross a silo, since the pipeline is what carries a worker to a distant occupation the credential distinctively opens. The two coefficients read on a common per-1\%-of-lift basis, differing only in the units of their response. For the OLS skill-distance outcome, a 1\% increase in lift is associated with approximately a $\beta$ percent increase in distance, the log--log coefficient reading as an elasticity. For the cross-silo LPM, the same 1\% increase is associated with approximately a $\beta/100$ percentage-point increase in the probability of crossing a silo, the raw per-log-unit coefficient divided by 100 to convert it to a per-1\% effect. The remoteness coefficient $\gamma$ is expected to be positive. Standard errors will be clustered on education and destination occupation.

Increment size enters as a second specification. Size and specificity are distinct properties of the credential event: size routes the worker into the non-local sample, specificity is what @eq-lift regresses distance on. They are not independent, and increment size is a rival explanation of the same variation rather than a confound in the backdoor sense --- a worker who moves from secondary school to a professional degree has repositioned further in human-capital space than one moving from a bachelor's to a master's, and may travel further for that reason alone, whatever channel they realize. Origin fixed effects do not absorb this, since two workers leaving the same 2016 occupation can carry very different increments. We therefore estimate @eq-lift augmented with a saturated set of increment-type dummies.

The dummy specification is defined only where an attainment change is observed, since only then is there an increment to code. Its committed cell is the proxy non-local sample, every observation of which recorded a change, so the saturated coding partitions it completely. There the question is whether $\beta$ survives holding increment type fixed: if specificity is what carries workers far, $\beta$ is identified within increment types, from the contrast between two workers whose credential change was structurally identical of whom one realized a high-lift path and one did not. We commit in advance to reading a substantial attenuation of $\beta$ under the dummies as a finding rather than a caveat. If $\beta$ collapses when increment type is held fixed, lift was proxying the size of the human-capital increment rather than the specificity of the channel it opens. We would report that as the finding.

The specification cannot run on the other three samples, for reasons that differ. The proxy local sample recorded no change at all, so there is nothing to code. The rescued non-local sample adds the reinstated workers, who activated a dormant credential with no recorded change; they have no codeable increment, and giving them a no-increment cell would absorb the pure-activation observations the rescue exists to add, defeating its purpose. The rescued local sample is predominantly zero-increment but carries one codeable group: the recorded-change non-activators the two-way adjustment demotes into it, workers who changed credential but whose destination lift did not clear activation. That group is a placebo, increment present and activation absent, so if the dummies bite there attainment magnitude moves workers regardless of activation, and if they do not a recorded increment does nothing without a pipeline. It would complete the dissociation the proxy non-local test begins. But the demoted subset's size is unknown until access and plausibly thin, and a null on an underpowered placebo is uninformative, indistinguishable from too few observations to detect an effect. We therefore report the placebo at access where the subset is large enough to estimate, and do not rely on it or count it among the committed fits.

The dummies are saturated on the attainment-level pair rather than on a level difference, because the ladder is ordinal and unevenly spaced: bachelor's-to-master's and secondary-to-college are both one step under a difference coding and are plainly not the same event. Each observed origin--destination attainment pair therefore receives its own indicator, with level-rise-without-field-change as the omitted reference, and a further indicator marks a field change across a two-digit CIP boundary, which enters alongside the level pairs rather than as a parallel category so that workers who change both are represented. Same-level field changes, which route non-local under @sec-rp with no attainment rise, fall out as the cell in which all level-pair indicators are zero and the field indicator is one. Cells that are structurally thin are collapsed under a rule fixed in advance and reported in @sec-AB. The attainment-transition counts that determine which cells are thin live in the linked file rather than the public table, so the collapse is applied at access; what is fixed in advance is the rule, not the collapse it produces. The increment-type coefficients are not of interest in themselves --- the specification exists to strip increment-size variation out of $\beta$, not to estimate it.

Age is excluded from the specification, and its exclusion is a modelling choice rather than a data limitation: age is recorded and available. The well-documented decline in occupational mobility with age [@topel1992job] operates, for jump distance, through the 2016 origin occupation: workers who acquire a new attainment later in life tend to start from a higher skill and hierarchy position than those completing the same credential early, so they sit closer to the credential's destination and travel a shorter measured distance. This is not a confound to be removed but the wormhole mechanism operating as intended, the credential carrying a worker the distance from their origin to the occupation it opens, with younger workers starting further away and travelling further. The channel is a property of where a worker starts, and the origin fixed effects $\delta_i$ absorb it along with every other origin-level determinant of distance. A separate age term is therefore neither needed nor clean: conditional on origin it carries no signal the mechanism predicts, and because age plausibly correlates with lift through selection into particular credential types, including it risks partialling out legitimate pipeline variation.

The model is evaluated across all four sample-classifications as described in @sec-data-vdl, with results reported for both the skill and cross-silo outcomes: four samples by two outcomes, eight base fits. The increment-type specification adds two more, the saturated dummies on the proxy non-local sample by two outcomes, for ten committed fits in the non-local section; the placebo version on the lift-adjusted local sample is reported at access if estimable and is not counted here. The within-$R^2$, the share of variance in the outcome explained by lift after partialling out origin fixed effects and destination remoteness, is not expected to be large in absolute terms: transition distance is inherently noisy and lift is an aggregate measure that captures only the systematic component of specificity-driven mobility. The relevant comparison is the ordering of within-$R^2$ across samples, not its absolute level.

The positive-distance restriction removes many apprenticeship completers, since NOC makes no distinction between apprentices and journeypeople of the same occupation: those already working in the target trade in 2016 show zero measured distance upon completion and are excluded by construction. Rather than threatening identification, this restriction improves measurement validity: the excluded zeros reflect occupation coarseness rather than true immobility, and their inclusion would introduce noise into the outcome variable. Workers who complete an entire apprenticeship program within the five-year window from a different 2016 occupation remain in the sample, and for these workers the wormhole mechanism is cleanly observable. The limitation is one of external validity rather than internal validity: estimates do not generalise to within-trade apprenticeship completers, whose human capital increment is real but invisible to NOC.

Beyond the apprenticeship case, the positive-distance restriction is also a selection on the outcome, but most of what it excludes is genuine immobility rather than a selection artifact. A true stayer contributes no distance to explain, so excluding stayers sets the scope of the conditional-on-positive estimand rather than selecting the surviving movers on anything, and the external-validity caveat above already covers it. The internal-validity concern is confined to the residual coarseness zeros, the real moves NOC records as zero distance, because OES predicts how often those occur as well as the distance conditional on moving. Insofar as the excluded zeros reflect coarseness rather than genuine immobility, the surviving positive subsample is selected on a margin the regressor also drives, with high-OES origins contributing their movers as a selected upper tail that the destination-side remoteness control does not absorb. The likely direction of that residual bias is attenuation, on the same logic as the local-sample leakage: the coarseness zeros are short measured moves, so resolving the coarseness would restore short high-OES moves that flatten the estimated specificity--distance gradient rather than steepen it. We therefore read the restricted estimate as attenuated, consistent with the lower-bound interpretation applied to the truncation in the limitations, and report it as such rather than as an unbiased effect.

### Predictions for the non-local model {#sec-non_local-predictions}

We commit in advance to six predictions for the non-local model, mirroring those for the local horse race and following from the wormhole mechanism rather than fitted to the data. Each applies to both outcomes, the OLS log skill distance and the LPM cross-silo indicator.

First, on the non-local sample, where a new attainment has become operative, the lift coefficient $\beta$ is positive: a stronger education--destination pipeline predicts a longer skill-distance move and a higher probability of crossing a silo. This is the relationship the model exists to estimate.

Second, on the local sample, where attainment is unchanged, the lift coefficient and the within-$R^2$ collapse toward zero relative to their non-local values. We do not require the local coefficient to be exactly zero, since a high-lift education can weakly compress local move distances even absent a new credential; the committed criterion is cross-sample degradation, stated and defended in @sec-non_local_false. This is the out-of-regime falsification, the mirror of the local horse race failing on the non-local sample.

Third, the lift adjustment sharpens the non-local estimate. Rescuing the misrouted wormholes into the non-local sample, and removing the recorded-but-non-activated moves from it, raises the lift coefficient and the within-$R^2$ relative to the proxy classification, because both operations replace mismatched observations with ones the mechanism predicts.

Fourth, the lift adjustment leaves the local estimate near zero. The moves the adjustment removes from the local sample are the leaked wormholes that would otherwise import a spurious lift--distance signal, so their removal can only hold the local coefficient at or below its already-degraded proxy value, never lift it. Predictions three and four together widen the non-local-versus-local gap under adjustment, strengthening the dissociation, exactly as the local horse race's fourth prediction widens its own gap.

Fifth, a spurious lift--distance relationship, one driven by a confound rather than by credential-contingent enablement, would appear in both samples, since a confound does not know which workers changed education. Its absence from the local coefficient, under both classifications, is what marks the relationship as credential-contingent rather than mechanical. This is the control that makes the falsification interpretable, the non-local analogue of binary's invariance in the local horse race.

Sixth, the lift coefficient survives conditioning on increment type. Estimated with the saturated increment-type dummies of @sec-non_local on the proxy non-local sample, where every observation records a change, $\beta$ remains positive and is not substantially attenuated relative to the primary specification, on both outcomes. This is the prediction that separates the two properties of the credential event, and the two accounts are not nested: increment size measures the magnitude of the human-capital gain without regard to where it directs the worker, and channel specificity is a distinct regressor rather than a restriction of it. What a surviving $\beta$ establishes is therefore that increment magnitude does not exhaust the variation, not that it is rejected. If $\beta$ instead collapses when increment type is held fixed, lift was proxying the size of the human-capital increment rather than the specificity of the channel it opens, and the wormhole is a statement about how much human capital a worker acquired rather than about where it directs them. We would report that as the finding. Where the demoted recorded-change subset of the lift-adjusted local sample is large enough to estimate, we additionally report the increment dummies there as a placebo: a null, increment type not predicting distance absent activation, would complete the dissociation from the other side. We do not rely on it, since its power is unknown until access.

### Out-of-Regime Falsification {#sec-non_local_false}

The non-local model is falsified in the local sample, where the highest
education attainment is unchanged. The criterion is the cross-sample degradation of the lift coefficient and the within-$R^2$, not their vanishing in absolute terms. Because lift enters on a common natural-log scale in every subsample, the $\beta$ estimate and the within-$R^2$ are directly comparable across subsamples, and the prediction is that both collapse from the non-local to the local sample. We do not require the local coefficient to be exactly zero: a high-lift education can compress local move distances weakly even absent a new credential, so the claim is degradation toward zero relative to the non-local estimate, consistent with the ordering-not-level standard applied to the within-$R^2$ throughout.

The collapse has two sources, and both are consistent with the wormhole
mechanism. Without a new highest attainment the wormhole channel is shut: the
worker's education is already reflected in their 2016 occupation, the starting
point of any local move, so it carries no additional predictive content for that
move, whereas the non-local education is acquired within the window and does its
repositioning where it can be observed. Second, high-lift transitions require a
worker to have moved into the occupation their credential distinctively feeds,
which without a new attainment is largely already reflected in the 2016
occupation, so high-lift realisations are truncated in the local sample and a
near-zero lift coefficient there reflects range restriction as much as a
switched-off mechanism. Neither reading threatens the falsification. A
spurious lift--distance relationship, one driven by a confound rather than
by credential-contingent enablement, would appear in both samples, since the
confound would not know which workers had changed education; its appearance in
neither the local coefficient nor anywhere a confound could hide is what marks
the relationship as credential-contingent rather than mechanical.

Two features of the local sample bear on its standing as a falsification sample.
It is large (most workers do not acquire a new highest attainment over the
inter-census period), so the null it delivers is precise rather than
underpowered, a well-powered absence of relationship rather than silence. It is
also subject to a modest contamination, because the partition variable is only a
proxy for the mechanism: what matters is whether the 2016 occupation is
informative, and "no substantial inter-census change in attainment" stands in for that.
Recorded highest attainment is in turn a lossy proxy for
the worker's actual position in human-capital space: any increment the record
fails to capture routes a genuinely repositioned worker into the local sample.
The failure takes several forms. A worker may earn a credential that does not
raise highest attainment, a sub-baccalaureate certificate, or a second field at
the same level, so that real training leaves the partition variable unmoved; a
nurse aide completing a practical-nursing certificate is one such case. Or the
timing may be wrong: a worker who earned their highest attainment shortly before
the 2016 reference week is formally local but holds a transitional rather than
credential-matched 2016 occupation, and so behaves like a non-local mover whose
jump straddles the census boundary. What unites these cases is not their cause
but their effect: the record misses a real increment, so the leakage cannot be
enumerated source by source, and the defense does not rest on cataloguing it.

The leakage is small, and the measurement-complete requirement removes one clear
class of it, excluding the graduates of intensive, occupationally specific programs, who
disproportionately lack a 2016 occupation at all. What matters more than any
filter is that whatever leakage remains works against the predicted dissociation
rather than producing it, for a reason that holds regardless of why the record
failed: a leaked mover imports wormhole behaviour, a long credential-driven move,
into the local sample, which the cost metrics assign low probability, so it degrades
the fit of skill and hierarchy while leaving binary unchanged. The leak thus favours
binary in the local horse race, the opposite of manufacturing the structured metrics'
in-regime advantage. This is the final reason the criterion is
stated as degradation and not as an absolute zero, which would be hostage to
precisely this contamination.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

### Local Mobility

Two sample restriction mechanisms introduce a potential selection 
concern for local mobility. Non-linkage and non-observability of 
occupation are both disproportionately concentrated among 
low-attachment workers, individuals with casual, seasonal, or 
intermittent employment whose identifying information is also less 
stable across census cycles, so the two filters largely co-select 
the same low-skill population rather than introducing independent 
exclusions. This shared exclusion affects the representativeness of 
population-level transition estimates (external validity) but does not 
threaten the internal validity of the horse race. For the horse race
results to be biased, the excluded workers' transitions would need to be 
systematically more or less rationalizable by a particular cost 
matrix than those of their observed counterparts in the same region 
of occupational space. No such mechanism is apparent: exclusion is 
driven by attachment instability and identifier churn, neither of 
which has a clear relationship to how well transitions conform to 
any particular cost structure conditional on occupation. The residual 
unlinked population among otherwise-observable workers, recent 
immigrants, young workers, and high-movers, similarly lacks any 
obvious occupational-space concentration that would differentially 
favour or penalize a particular metric.

A notable omitted factor for local mobility  is \emph{path-specific} wage differentials. The additively separable component of wage gains, recoverable from origin and destination wage levels alone, is absorbed by the 
margins insofar as high-wage destinations attract larger inflows and 
low-wage origins larger outflows. The residual dyadic component, 
reflecting transition-specific wage premia and discounts beyond what 
origin and destination wage levels predict, is an omitted factor. 
Short-distance transitions are within a similar occupational 
neighbourhood, reducing employer uncertainty about candidate fit and 
productivity; long-distance transitions cross larger skill or 
hierarchical gaps, and employers may discount wage offers to 
compensate for that uncertainty, or workers may accept lower wages 
to gain entry to a distant occupation.

Thus, path-specific wage differentials are better understood as an 
alternative mechanism, rather than a confounder. If employers use the same metric that governs mobility to assess candidate fit uncertainty, discounting wages for transitions that are long under the winning metric, that discount reinforces worker selection toward shorter transitions under 
the same metric. Both channels predict identical patterns of 
transitions and are equally consistent with the winning metric being 
the correct description of the mobility geometry. The horse race 
identifies which distance geometry best rationalizes observed 
transitions in a reduced-form sense, but cannot separately attribute 
that rationalization to worker or employer preferences regarding 
distance.

### Non-Local Mobility {#sec-non_local-limits}

The non-local regime studies non-negative operative increments, as defined in @sec-rp: transitions where the operative credential rises above the worker's prior ceiling or respecifies at the same level. Substitutive moves, where an over-credentialed worker retrains below their ceiling and repositions on a sub-maximal credential, lie outside the estimand and are invisible to a highest-attainment record; the findings therefore speak to additive and lateral specific-human-capital activation, not to occupational mobility of every kind. This is a scope of the question rather than a gap in the answer, and it is consistent with the paper's premise that mobility is not one thing: the substitutive channel is a distinct phenomenon with its own economics, deserving its own treatment rather than absorption into this one.

The non-local partition is restricted to individuals who acquire a new highest educational attainment between 2016 and 2021 and report an occupation in both periods. A 2016 occupation is observed if and only if the individual was employed between May 1st and 7th, the 2016 census reference week. For the 2015/2016 school year, roughly half of 18-29 year old students reported concurrent work, with an (unweighted) ten percentage point decrease for university students, consistent with more intensive programs suppressing concurrent employment.^[source: Statistics Canada table 37-10-0104-01.] The Census reference week provides a partial offset: falling after the typical post-secondary academic year ends, it captures individuals who have recently finished exams and may have already begun summer employment. But this offset is weaker for intensive professional programs that are either year-round or have students for whom summer employment is atypical. The resulting truncation is not random: missingness is concentrated among the most occupationally specific educations, precisely the credentials that anchor the highest-lift pipelines, where the wormhole mechanism is strongest and jumps are longest. Thus estimates are attenuated toward zero and should be interpreted as lower bounds on the true relationship, given that truncation is concentrated precisely where the signal is strongest. Notably, this missingness pattern is not purely a limitation: the disproportionate absence of 2016 occupations among the most specific credentials is itself consistent with the wormhole mechanism, since program intensity and specificity are precisely what suppresses concurrent employment. In the online companion we plot each education's occupational specificity against the share of its workers missing a 2016 occupation, quantifying the magnitude of this truncation.

The specificity regression faces an analogous identification 
challenge to the horse race. Lift is observed and enters the 
regression, but cannot distinguish between two mechanisms that 
predict identical patterns. A specific education opens doors to 
particular distant occupations that a general education does not: 
the human capital match is narrow, so only a subset of distant 
destinations become reachable following attainment (enablement). At 
the same time, workers with specific educations may face stronger 
incentives to seek out distant occupations where those skills are 
scarce and rewarded, making long-distance moves financially attractive 
relative to staying within a crowded local neighbourhood (motivation). 
Because both channels operate through the same pipelines that lift 
measures, the reduced-form estimate conflates the two and cannot be separately 
attributed to either. The regression should therefore be interpreted 
as identifying the reduced-form predictive relationship between 
pipeline strength and distance traveled, without attribution to a specific 
mechanism, though the estimate remains informative: if either 
channel is operative, the regression will detect it.

## Conclusion

- What we found \[PLACEHOLDER: awaiting data\]

The central policy takeaway from this analysis is that labour market adjustment mechanisms are not one-size-fits-all: the appropriate intervention depends on which mobility regime contains the occupation experiencing a shortage. The three mobility sub-regimes suggest three distinct policy levers.

In the Skill sub-regime, reskilling and short-cycle training are the natural adjustment mechanisms. Workers in adjacent occupations already possess much of the relevant task content, and targeted reskilling can accelerate the reallocation of labour toward occupations in shortage without requiring formal retraining. The policy implication is that investment in modular, portable training that builds on existing skill profiles will generate the largest mobility response in this segment.

In the Hierarchy sub-regime, the relevant bottleneck is not skill transferability but the hierarchy's silo and platform structure. An occupational shortage within one silo cannot be addressed by upskilling workers from a different silo, even if the occupations share a near-identical skill profile. Instead, shortages are addressed within the silo, through lateral movement across a platform and, where the step up requires no credential, movement to an adjacent one. Where the upward step is credential-gated, it is not a within-silo mobility problem at all but a program-capacity one, and belongs to the lever of the Binary sub-regime below: the gating credential is acquired through a specific program whose entrants are drawn from across the labour market, so relief comes from expanding that program rather than from moving incumbents up the silo. Bridging programs, mentorship structures, and targeted recruitment across platforms of the same silo are the appropriate instruments for the uncredentialed steps.

In the Binary sub-regime, either a worker has the required education, or they do not. Neither reskilling nor within-silo movement can substitute for education. Adjustment in this sub-regime depends entirely on expanding formal training pipelines: increasing capacity in the relevant educational programs, reducing barriers to program entry, and shortening time-to-completion where possible. These are also the occupations that immigration policy should target, both in terms of admission and rapid credential recognition. 

If the hypothesized sub-regime structure is confirmed, the geometry of occupational mobility determines which policy lever to pull, and the wrong lever is not just ineffective but potentially counterproductive.

## O\*NET to NOC 2021 Skill Mapping {#sec-AA}

OaSIS provides occupation-level skill profiles for Canadian
classifications and would be an attractive data source for constructing
$C_{\text{skill}}$. However, OaSIS does not expose how those profiles
are constructed: the mapping between O\*NET and NOC 2021 occupations is not observable, the weights linking underlying occupations are not published, and there is no information on how multiple O\*NET occupations are combined to form an occupation profile. This appendix describes an alternative mapping constructed explicitly from published crosswalks, allowing full transparency of inputs and weights, diagnostic evaluation of mapping quality, and reproducibility of all outputs.

The mapping chains four classifications: O\*NET 2019 $\rightarrow$ SOC
2018 $\rightarrow$ NOC 2016 $\rightarrow$ NOC 2021. Each stage introduces potential one-to-many relationships. A naive approach would assign equal weight to all admissible paths, but this leads to over-weighting of occupations that appear frequently in crosswalk chains and inclusion of unrelated occupations. Instead, path weights are constructed to reflect the degree of splitting at each stage: if a source occupation splits into $n_s$ destination occupations at stage $s$, each path through that stage receives weight $w_s = 1/n_s$, and the overall path weight is $w_{\text{path}} = w_1 \times w_2 \times w_3$. Path weights are then aggregated by origin O\*NET occupation and destination NOC 2021 code and normalized to sum to one within each NOC to yield base weights. The consequences of naive versus path weighting can be severe: for NOC 72600 (Air pilots, flight engineers and flying instructors), naive weights assign five-eighths of the skill profile to agricultural workers, while path weights assign 78\% to pilots.

A power transformation and renormalization is then applied to further
reduce the influence of mapping artifacts: $\tilde{w}_k \propto w_k^2$.
This concentrates weight on the dominant O\*NET contributors and
diminishes the influence of peripheral occupations that enter through
crosswalk chains with many splits. For NOC 72600, downweighting
increases the pilot share of the skill profile to 96\%. Each O\*NET
occupation is then represented as a point in a reduced skill space using the first 12 principal components of the O\*NET skill content variables, and for each NOC 2021 code the weighted centroid of its contributing O\*NET occupations is computed using the downweighted mapping, yielding a 12-dimensional skill profile for each NOC occupation.

Two diagnostics assess the quality of each occupation's mapping in skill space. Herfindahl concentration measures how concentrated the mapping weights are across contributing O\*NET occupations: $H = \sum_k \tilde{w}_k^2$. For example, a Herfindahl of $\frac{2}{3}$ indicates that the occupation skill profile is effectively dominated by a single O\*NET occupation with a weight of $\approx .8$.  In contrast, when $H=\frac{1}{3}$ the largest contributor's share is between $\frac13$ and $\sqrt{\frac13}=.58$. Scaled Similarity measures the internal coherence of the contributing occupations in skill space: the weighted average distance of each contributing O\*NET occupation from the occupation centroid is computed, then normalized to a $[0.05, 1]$ interval by dividing by the maximum value across all occupations, multiplying by 0.95, and subtracting from 1, so that $SS = 1 - 0.95 \times \bar{d} / \max_j \bar{d}_j$. The lower bound of 0.05 is chosen to match the approximate lower bound of the Herfindahl index, making the two measures' floors commensurable. The mapping quality composite is the product $H \times SS$, which is high only when the mapping is both concentrated and internally coherent. The three interpretation cases are: high $H$ with any $SS$ (no problem, almost all weight on a single O\*NET occupation); low $H$ with high $SS$ (no problem, diffuse but coherent); and low $H$ with low $SS$ (problematic, a diffuse average of disparate occupations whose skill profile is unreliable). NOC 41200 (University professors and lecturers) is a canonical example of the third case.

The six occupations ranked below the verified benchmark 72600 (see @sec-data-public) are excluded from the local and non-local samples. The full mapping pipeline is implemented in [@onet_to_noc] and is constructed entirely from O\*NET data and published crosswalks.

Because NOC is in places a finer classification than O\*NET, some distinct NOC unit groups inherit the same O\*NET profile and so sit at zero skill distance from one another: see @tbl-zero-skill-groups for a summary of the groups.  Grouping occupations by shared profile yields `r zeros_components$no` such groups, spanning `r zeros_tabyl$total[1]` occupations and accounting for the `r zeros_components$num_zero_off_diagonal` zero off-diagonal cells noted in @sec-cost-metrics:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-zero-skill-groups
#| tbl-cap: "Zero skill distance groups."

zeros_tabyl|>
  select(group_size, n, percent)|>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(percent), decimals = 1) |>
  cols_label(
    group_size = "Group Size",
    n = "Number",
    percent = "Percent"
  ) |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = "90%", data_row.padding = px(4)) 
```

The group of twelve is the processing and manufacturing supervisors, which NOC distinguishes by industry (supervisors of food and beverage processing, of plastic and rubber products, of motor vehicle assembling, and so on) but which O\*NET represents as a single first-line production supervisor occupation, onto which all twelve map with a Herfindahl concentration of one. Their shared profile is therefore not a symptom of noisy mapping but the opposite: the twelve are among the most cleanly mapped occupations in the matrix, and their zero mutual distances reflect O\*NET's occupational resolution rather than any deficiency in the crosswalk. Eleven of the twelve share the same broad category, where the hierarchical metric also places them close (distance one or two), so the two geometries agree that these occupations are near. The twelfth, 72022 (supervisors, printing and related occupations), sits in a different broad category, so the hierarchical metric assigns it the cross-category sentinel of nine to each of the other eleven while the skill metric assigns zero. This is the widest disagreement the two geometries admit, on a set of occupations the horse race assigns to the Hierarchy sub-regime; whether the skill reading or the hierarchical reading better rationalizes the observed transitions among these supervisors is precisely what the local model adjudicates.

## Lift construction {#sec-AB}

Lift is the cell-level term inside the education-side KL divergence $\text{KL}(P(\text{NOC}\mid e)\,\|\,P(\text{NOC}))$: where that divergence summarises how distinctive an education's whole occupation distribution is, lift reads a single education--occupation cell, how distinctively this education feeds this occupation. It is high where an education channels into an occupation far more than baseline, near one where it is no more likely than average to lead there, and below one where it leads there less than baseline.

Lift $m(e,n) = P(\text{NOC}=n\mid \text{education}=e)/P(\text{NOC}=n)$ is estimated from the census education$\times$NOC table (98-10-0404-01, described in @sec-data-public), and two features of that table make the raw ratio unstable in thin cells: the conditional $P(n\mid e)$ is a sample proportion, noisy when few workers hold education $e$, and the published counts are randomly rounded to base five, so a small cell's value is dominated by rounding. We address the two separately.

For the sampling noise, we smooth the conditional with a Dirichlet prior centred on the marginal occupation distribution:
$$\hat P(n\mid e) = \frac{c_{en} + \alpha\, P(n)}{T_e + \alpha},$$
where $c_{en}$ is the count of education-$e$ workers in occupation $n$, $T_e = \sum_n c_{en}$, and $\alpha$ is the prior strength in pseudo-workers. The prior is the marginal $P(n)$, so an education with no information is pulled toward "no pipeline" ($m \to 1$), and the pull is proportional to ignorance: a thin education ($T_e$ small relative to $\alpha$) is shrunk hard, a well-populated one ($T_e \gg \alpha$) is left essentially untouched. Because the prior is the same $P(n)$ that appears in the denominator of lift, the shrinkage target is exactly the ratio's neutral point, and a fully shrunk cell has lift one by construction. We shrink only the numerator; the denominator $P(n)$, estimated from the full table, is left raw, so that genuine pipelines into rare occupations, where a small $P(n)$ produces a large lift, are preserved rather than flattened. We set $\alpha = 15$, chosen so that the ranking of the strongest pipelines is stable: raising $\alpha$ far higher, to 1000, leaves the top of the ranking unchanged, since those pipelines are driven by the raw denominator rather than by numerator noise, while $\alpha = 15$ leaves well-populated cells such as optometry (education total near seven thousand) shrunk by under a percent.

For the rounding, we require a minimum realised cell count. A cell with $c_{en} = 15$ has a relative standard error near $1/\sqrt{15} \approx 26\%$ from sampling alone, above Statistics Canada's own "use with caution" threshold, and base-five rounding adds error of the same order; below roughly this count the estimated lift reflects noise and rounding rather than a real pipeline. Inspection of the public table shows that the correspondence a high lift is meant to capture is itself unreliable well above that point: among high-lift cells, those with counts in the low tens are frequently incoherent pairings that clear the ratio by small-sample chance, while by a count of a few hundred the high-lift pairs are almost uniformly genuine pipelines. We therefore set the floor at $c_{en} \ge 100$, where the sampling relative standard error is near ten percent, comfortably below Statistics Canada's caution threshold, and the high-lift correspondence is coherent. Cells below the floor are treated as unmeasured rather than as low-lift, since the ratio there is not a reliable estimate of anything, and workers whose education--destination cell falls below the floor carry no lift value. This is a reliability standard on the construction of the regressor, fixed in advance on the public table, blind to any transition distance. The unfiltered ratio, which is a mismeasurement rather than a weaker measurement, is not an alternative we entertain.

The floor is fixed at $100$ rather than swept, and two facts on the public table establish that $100$ is neither too low nor worth raising. It is not too low: the sampling relative standard error at the floor is near ten percent and the Dirichlet prior displaces the estimate by a comparable amount, both small against the spread of log lift, which runs across roughly thirteen units from the anti-associated tail to the strongest pipelines, so a cell at the floor is neither noise-dominated nor prior-dominated relative to the variation the regressor must resolve. It is not worth raising: moving the floor from $100$ to $200$ removes about two percent of the activated sample, a slice already shown reliable by the same standard, so a higher floor would discard usable observations without adding reliability the estimates lack. Because $100$ is defensible on reliability alone and the sample it admits is already reliable, the floor is held fixed and robustness is assessed on the activation threshold $\tau$ (@sec-AD), the parameter of the rule rather than of the measurement.

Lift enters the regression in natural logarithm. The log is the natural scale for a multiplicative quantity whose neutral point is one: equal ratios become equal distances, the long right tail of rare-destination pipelines is compressed onto a comparable scale with ordinary moves, its neutral point at $\log m = 0$ marks a pipeline no stronger than baseline, and paired with the log outcome the coefficient reads as an elasticity. Because the same natural-log scale is applied in every subsample, the coefficient and within-$R^2$ are directly comparable across them. The Dirichlet floor guarantees the smoothed lift is strictly positive, so the log is always defined.

## CWTVD resolving power  {#sec-AC}

@sec-local adjudicates the horse race on the likelihood criterion and the
geometry-aware criterion, the latter scored under each informative judge,
and a win requires leading on all of them. The role of $\Delta CWTVD$ as a
co-equal geometry-aware criterion rests on a property established here by
simulation: among the two correlated informative geometries, $\Delta CWTVD$
resolves which governs more sharply than $\Delta KL$ does. This appendix
substantiates that property and states why it can be established only by
simulation.
 
The [online companion](https://rpmartin.github.io/not-one-thing-companion#sec-higher-resolution) plots improvement relative to
independence against $\varepsilon$ for each candidate metric, across three
mixed data-generating processes (columns) and the three criteria (rows):
$\Delta CWTVD$ scored under $C_{\mathrm{hierarchy}}$, $\Delta CWTVD$ scored
under $C_{\mathrm{skill}}$, and $\Delta KL$. Read down a column, the two
$\Delta CWTVD$ rows agree on which geometry peaks highest in every mixture:
skill in the skill-heavy $75/25$ column, hierarchy in the hierarchy-heavy
$25/75$ column, whichever the true mixture favours at $50/50$. The winner
is the same under either scoring endpoint, so a metric that leads under one
informative judge leads under the other and, by the bracketing argument in
@sec-local, under every blend between them. This agreement is the
robustness the two-endpoint criterion is meant to certify, not a
degeneracy: the endpoints coincide on the winner while remaining far enough
apart in construction, $\mathrm{corr}(C_{\mathrm{skill}},
C_{\mathrm{hierarchy}}) = 0.3$, that coincidence is informative.

The contrast with $\Delta KL$ is the resolving-power property. Under either
$\Delta CWTVD$ scoring the gap between the skill and hierarchy peaks tracks
the imbalance of the true mixture, widening as the mixture departs from
balance. $\Delta KL$ holds the two curves close to coincident across all
three mixtures, resolving the imbalanced cases only weakly. A second
difference appears at the benchmark: under every mixture the $\Delta KL$
curve for $C_{\mathrm{binary}}$ retains a positive tail well past its peak,
the same geometry-blind credit for the aggregate stay/move split that
drives the out-of-regime KL behaviour in @sec-local-falsification; both
$\Delta CWTVD$ rows strip that credit out and the $C_{\mathrm{binary}}$
tail collapses to the independence line. Both features point the same way:
$\Delta CWTVD$ separates the two correlated geometries more sharply and
denies the benchmark credit it has not earned geometrically.

The simulations also exhibit the wrong-bet penalty that the out-of-regime
falsification relies on. In the $25/75$ column scored under
$C_{\mathrm{hierarchy}}$, skill is the minority geometry graded by its
rival's judge, and its peak falls below the $C_{\mathrm{binary}}$
benchmark; scored under $C_{\mathrm{skill}}$ it recovers above binary. A
metric making a geometric bet is penalised by distance for making the wrong
one, where binary, making no off-diagonal bet, cannot be. This is the
in-sample analogue of the below-independence crossing predicted in
@sec-local-falsification, with binary in place of independence as the
reference, and it corroborates the mechanism under known
data-generating processes rather than testing it.
 

This resolving-power property is established under known data-generating
processes rather than read off the estimation sample, for the structural
reason given in @sec-local: the property is a statement about the mapping
from a known true mixture to the measured gap between criteria, and a
single observed labour market delivers one gap drawn from one unknown
mixture, with no reference mixture against which its magnitude could be
judged. The Monte Carlo is therefore the complete justification the claim
admits, not preliminary evidence awaiting empirical corroboration. The
figures here substantiate the property; @sec-local states what follows for
trusting $\Delta CWTVD$ when it parts from $\Delta KL$ on the Canadian
data.
 
## Threshold sensitivity for latent-activation reinstatement {#sec-AD}

The local/non-local partition routes on the recorded education change, a proxy for whether a large human-capital increment became operative within the window (@sec-rp). Latent activation is one of the proxy's two known failures, and the only one that commits to a threshold: reclassification on the reverse error turns on $\log m = 0$, a property of the measure, so it has no parameter whose sensitivity needs reporting. This appendix therefore treats latent activation alone, identifying those workers from what is observed and reinstating them into the non-local sample as a robustness check on the specificity--distance estimates. It is a correction to measurement error in the partition variable, not a headline result, and the reinstated estimate is reported only beside the uncorrected one.

The reason the exercise is worth running, rather than signing the selection by
argument, is that the sign is genuinely ambiguous a priori. The non-local sample
loses whichever latent activators failed to produce a recorded change, and which
workers those are depends on how the holding-out ends. A graduate who takes the
first offer activates promptly, their move coincides with the recorded
credential, and they stay non-local. A graduate who holds out activates late,
often only after the credential has aged into a prior cycle as recorded
attainment, so their move shows no change and drops to local. If the wait ends
in the distant match it was for, the droppers are disproportionately the long
jumps, and their loss selects the non-local sample toward shorter moves,
attenuating the specificity--distance slope. If the wait instead ends in
capitulation, the worker settling for an occupation near the one held before the
credential, the droppers are the short movers, and their loss selects the sample
toward longer moves, inflating it. Both outcomes begin in the same behaviour and
the record distinguishes neither, since in both the credential is old and the
move is unaccompanied by a recorded change. No argument from the record resolves
this, but the reinstatement does, because the dropped workers and their distances
are observed.

The signature of activation is a within-worker change in whether the occupation
uses the standing credential, with the credential held fixed. We read
credential--occupation match by the same lift $m(e,n) = P(\text{NOC}=n \mid \text{education}=e)/P(\text{NOC}=n)$ that serves as the non-local regressor, so the wedge reclassification and the non-local model are built on one quantity. Match is $m$ high, non-match $m$ low, with $m = 1$ the baseline at which an education feeds an occupation no more than the occupation's overall prevalence would predict.

A worker with unchanged education $e$ is reinstated when the credential is
dormant at the origin and a genuine pipeline at the destination:
$$\log m(e, n_{2016}) < 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \log m(e, n_{2021}) \ge \tau ,$$
with the destination cell required to clear the reliability floor of @sec-AB.
The first condition fixes the origin as genuinely non-matching, below-baseline
lift, and is a gate held at baseline. The second declares the destination a
pipeline of strength at least $\tau$ on the log-lift scale. The reliability floor
is not a third criterion for activation but a precondition on reading lift at
all, and it lives with the lift construction of @sec-AB rather than with the
rule; $\tau$ is the sole parameter of the activation criterion itself, and it is
the axis varied below, the floor being held fixed at its reliability-justified value. The gate conditions only on the 2016 occupation, which
does not enter the specificity equation; the pipeline condition uses the 2021
occupation, which is destination-side and so shares information with destination
OES, a regressor. Membership is the contrast of the two, so workers reaching the
same 2021 occupation are separated on their 2016 state, but the destination leg
is not wholly clean and the sensitivity to $\tau$ and to the count floor is what
certifies the correction is not manufactured by it.

We report the reinstated count alongside the reinstated non-local slope, beside
the uncorrected slope, across the threshold $\tau \in \{2, 3, 4\}$ on log lift, with
$\tau = 2$ the primary value. The reliability floor is held fixed at $100$ rather
than varied: @sec-AB shows that at this count neither sampling noise nor the
Dirichlet prior displaces the estimate materially against the spread of log lift,
so cells at the floor are already reliable, and raising it would discard a
reliable slice of the sample without buying reliability the estimates lack. The
activation threshold, by contrast, is the parameter of the rule itself, and it
is the axis the robustness sweep varies. The sweep is reported in full; we do not
select a value after seeing the estimates. The threshold is fixed on the
definition of activation, a genuine dormant-to-pipeline switch, and is not tuned
toward moving the slope; moving it is neither the aim nor a success condition. The
maintained expectation is the opposite: latent activation is a leak we expect to
be small, so a small reinstated count together with a slope stable against the
uncorrected estimate is the affirmative outcome, evidence that the record-change
partition is not materially contaminated by this failure. A slope stable across
the sweep, and across tightening the dormant-origin gate below baseline, indicates
the correction does not turn on the destination leg or on the threshold; a slope
that moves only at permissive $\tau$ locates the sensitivity; a large reinstated
count that moved the slope substantially would instead be evidence the partition
had been materially wrong, the one outcome that would count against the
uncorrected estimate. Because the count is reported rather than engineered, a small count is
read as latent activation being empirically rare, itself consistent with the
mechanism, since a worker already holding their highest credential is unlikely
to leave it dormant and then activate it within a five-year window.

Where the reinstated count is large enough to be informative, the observed
distances of the reinstated workers also resolve the sign left ambiguous above:
whether latent activators are the long jumps a selective search strands in the
local sample, or the short jumps a quality gradient leaves behind, is read
directly from whether their reinstatement raises or lowers the non-local slope.
Where the count is small, that sign is left unresolved, but immaterially so,
since a leak too small to move the estimate does not need its direction fixed.

## Sparse-cell calibration and detection power {#sec-AE}

Two sub-regime readings depend on whether a horse race run on few observations can be trusted: the high-OES Binary subset of @sec-subregime-predictions, where thin off-diagonal mass raises the worry that a binary win is manufactured rather than real, and the 40-and-over age band of the same section, where a low move rate raises the mirror worry that a graded winner present in the data would go undetected and leave binary winning by default. Both are settled by simulation at the affected subset's realized count, and both procedures are fixed here in advance; neither can be executed before access, since each requires margins and effect sizes observed only in the linked file.

The two readings guard against opposite errors and so require opposite generating truths. The first is a false-positive question: when no geometry governs, how often does noise alone fake a decisive gap? We generate under a truth that sits exactly between the two informative geometries, the balanced cost $C = \tfrac{1}{2}(C_{\text{skill}}/7.145) + \tfrac{1}{2}(C_{\text{hierarchy}}/3)$, so that neither graded metric should win by construction. We solve the transport plan under this cost against the subset's realized margins at the reference $\varepsilon$, draw one thousand synthetic flows from it as a single multinomial over all cells at the subset's total count $N$, and on each synthetic flow run the horse race exactly as on real data, scoring each metric against that sample's own independence baseline and taking each metric's peak over the $\varepsilon$ sweep. We record the fraction of samples in which the peak gap between the two graded metrics exceeds the ten percent threshold. If fewer than five percent do, the threshold is safe against noise at this count and the subset's verdict is read normally; if more do, the subset is noise-limited and its verdict is not read. This is the reading committed for the high-OES Binary subset: it establishes that a decisive gap there is unlikely to be an artifact of sparse cells.

The second is a power question, and it is what the 40-and-over band requires: if a graded metric genuinely governed at a realistic strength, would a race on this few moves recover it? Here the generating truth is not the balanced mixture but each graded geometry in turn. We generate under $C_{\text{skill}}$ alone at the effect size skill exhibits in the band where it governs, thin to the old band's realized move count, run the identical race, and record how often skill is recovered as the winner; we then repeat under $C_{\text{hierarchy}}$ alone at the strength hierarchy shows where it governs. The band is adequately powered only if both graded signals would have been recovered at its move count. If both would have and the data nonetheless favour binary, the binary result is substantive: the rivals had their chance and did not take it. If either graded signal would have been missed, a binary win cannot exclude a hidden signal of that kind, and we report the band as underpowered against that rival rather than as evidence that binary governs. The effect sizes anchoring these runs are observed only at access, in the bands where each graded metric wins, which is why the power check is a committed procedure rather than a result stated here.

The two halves share all machinery and differ only in the generating truth and the quantity recorded: the balanced mixture with a false-positive rate for calibration, each pure graded geometry with a recovery rate for power. A subset is read only if it passes the check its inference depends on, calibration for the high-OES Binary subset and power for the oldest age band.
